summary: A hybrid charge quantum interference device (h-CQUID) combining Josephson junctions with a high kinetic-inductance NbN loop demonstrates control of fluxon tunneling via the Aharonov-Casher effect, with the interference between two tunneling paths modulated by charge on a superconducting island. At destructive interference conditions ($Q = 2e(n + 1/2)$), the phase-slip energy $E_S$ is suppressed, with minimum $E_S/h \approx 0.4$ GHz achieved for asymmetric junctions with $\nu_1 = 1.48$ GHz and $\nu_2 = 1.08$ GHz tunneling rates.
motivation: The h-CQUID architecture addresses fabrication limitations of earlier CQUID designs that relied on 10 nm nanowires (fabrication accuracy $\pm 2$ nm) with highly variable phase-slip energy; Josephson junctions offer $>90\%$ parameter reproducibility and can be cleanly integrated with kinetic-inductance films.
method: Two Josephson junctions with a superconducting aluminum island between them were embedded in a compact NbN loop ($L_k \approx 81.3$ nH, $L_{\square} \sim 1.6$ nH/sq, grown by atomic layer deposition) and coupled inductively to a $\lambda/2$ resonator at 10.676 GHz; two-tone spectroscopy and Rabi oscillations were measured at 12 mK in a dilution refrigerator.
result: Two-tone spectroscopy shows periodic modulation with period $2e$ in the excitation energy $\Delta E = \sqrt{\epsilon(\Phi)^2 + E_S(Q)^2}$ as gate voltage varies the island charge $Q = C_g V_g$; the persistent current is $I_P \sim 11.5$ nA with $T_1 \approx 20$ ns, though quasiparticle poisoning in the NbN film creates parasitic charge-parity states that prevent complete suppression of tunneling.
